COMPOSITION PRIORITY: a distant environmental panning photograph with a small car, matching a wide street scene rather than a vehicle advertisement close-up. The complete vehicle bounding box must occupy only 38–44% of frame width and approximately 16–22% of frame height in square or portrait output; in horizontal output use the same width target with natural vehicle proportions. Place the car in the upper-middle band, with its roof around 31% and tire contact around 51% of image height. Pull the tracking camera substantially farther back; do not use a close low-angle hero shot. The foreground road should occupy roughly the lower half of the image and remain dark, calm and free for typography. Architecture fills the upper background with almost no sky (0–5%). Keep the complete vehicle and branding clear of the selected typography area. Preserve the attached car geometry but ignore its tight reference crop. Do not enlarge the car to fill the composition.

This is an image-editing/background-replacement task, not a request to generate or redraw a new car from scratch. Use the original vehicle cutout wherever possible, compositing it into a photorealistic urban campaign photograph. Protect the car body and branding; replace or extend the surroundings, then integrate road contact shadows, lighting and panning effects around the original vehicle. If your tool supports masks, mask the surroundings for replacement while protecting the vehicle. Do not claim that a generative edit guarantees pixel-identical preservation; for exact branding, retain/composite the original car pixels rather than repainting the livery. Preserve the exact white sedan model, body proportions, wheels, grille, lights, windows, and WB Taxi livery from the reference, including the magenta/violet panel arrangement, door wordmark and number 260. Do not mirror, redesign or replace the car.

Windows and cabin: keep all windows fully closed. Use realistic dark reflective glazing, natural reflections of the surrounding architecture and sky, and a deeply shadowed cabin so no face is identifiable through the windshield or side windows. Preserve window transparency cues, glass edges and believable reflections; do not paint flat opaque black panels over the glass. If an occupant is visible at all, show only an indistinct silhouette behind the reflections, with no discernible eyes, mouth or facial features. Do not invent a visible driver portrait, open the window, brighten the cabin or expose a distorted face. Apply this to every angle, including front three-quarter views. Preserve the reference vehicle silhouette, mirrors and window geometry.

Omit the blank white front license plate and its mounting bracket: continue the grille pattern naturally behind it. Do not add any blank white number plates or placeholder rectangles at the front or rear.

Camera: a distant environment-led tracking shot from around door-handle height, with a level camera and natural 35–50 mm perspective; no upward-looking wide-angle hero perspective. For the closest match choose the front-left three-quarter car reference, with the nose pointing left; preserve the selected reference angle and vehicle geometry. Keep the car small in the upper-middle of the frame and extend the road foreground for typography, respecting the selected layout safe area. Selected vehicle view: front-left three-quarter view, matching the reference viewpoint. Use the low, wide camera treatment described above. Show the entire vehicle, both bumpers and wheels, with breathing room around it.

Scene: a broad urban avenue beside one monumental modern facade, with tall pale stone piers, broad glass bays and a deep recessed dark ground floor. Frame architecture behind the car as indistinct broad masses, with every pier and glass bay heavily swept into horizontal tracking streaks; no crisp stone joints, sharp window mullions or clearly readable facade grid; show very little sky and no distant skyline, trees or street clutter. Clean urban architecture and open blue sky only: simple building facades, road surfaces and uncluttered sidewalks. No trees, foliage, bushes, parks or greenery in the background, through the windows, in reflections or in motion blur. Do not copy incidental greenery from a reference. The selected street scene determines the architecture: do not replace walls, underpasses or open-road surroundings with a row of modern apartment buildings. If buildings are present, use just one or two broad, simple facade masses with large neutral surfaces. Suppress small windows, repetitive sharp facade grids, ornamental details, sharp distant skylines, street furniture and clusters of poles. Buildings are atmospheric color and light bands rather than an architectural subject. No crowds, prominent advertising, busy signage, traffic clutter or foreground obstructions.

Motion and light: the camera tracks the moving car at matching speed in a realistic panning shot. Keep the original car body and branding sharp and unchanged; show clearly visible rotational motion blur in the wheels and strong, long, coherent horizontal panning streaks across BOTH the building facades and road. Background windows, facade edges and road markings must visibly stretch into soft directional bands at normal viewing size. Gentle shallow depth of field or a slightly blurred road alone is not enough: the architecture must lose fine detail through motion. Aim for a slow-shutter tracking photograph, approximately 1/15–1/30 second, with the car tracked sharply. Keep the bodywork, WB Taxi wordmark, number 260 and every magenta/violet livery boundary tack sharp: no blur, smearing, warped letters, redrawn logos or altered graphic details on the car. Protect the original branded body pixels; apply motion blur only to separate background/road and wheel regions. If the tool cannot preserve the logo pixels exactly, retain the original car as a composited layer rather than regenerating its branding. warm low-angle sunset sunlight from the side, long realistic tire shadows and golden reflections on the body, with soft amber light on simple facades and a clear cloudless sky. Keep white paint believable and magenta/violet branding accurate; no heavy orange grading, artificial colored lighting or night scene. warm cream and champagne highlights on the architecture, deep desaturated petrol-green and charcoal shadows, and predominantly dark charcoal/petrol-green asphalt with only narrow restrained golden highlights near the tires. Keep the lower half roughly 1.5–2 stops darker than the sunlit car; no broad bright amber road, washed-out gray foreground or glossy golden carpet. The green belongs only to shadow grading, never foliage. Keep white paint neutral and the original magenta/violet livery accurate. Extreme slow-shutter panning, approximately 1/8–1/15 second: strong long horizontal motion streaks across the entire facade and diagonal perspective streaks across the foreground road. At normal viewing size the architecture is broad abstract light and shadow bands, not a readable building with a merely softened edge; rotational wheel blur, with the branded body sharp. Use directional warm sunlight for sunset; when Day is selected retain neutral daylight and the same deep cool shadows; for Evening replace sunlight with cool blue-hour ambient light and restrained warm architectural illumination Use neutral urban colors and rich violet/magenta brand accents. Match the cinematic, natural photographic finish of the existing moving taxi campaign photo. Realistic tire contact and road shadow; no floating car, distorted geometry, radial zoom blur, speed-line graphics or blur across the branded bodywork.

Output aspect ratio 4:5. Compose the scene with a clean, low-detail typography-safe area in the lower 40% of the image. Extend the environment rather than filling the frame with the subject: use uncluttered sky, architecture, cabin surfaces or softly blurred road, with calm tonal contrast. Place the main subject outside this area; keep faces, hands, the complete car and its branding clear of future text. No generated text, placeholder lettering, graphic panels or artificial blank borders.  Leave the reserved area usable for a headline, supporting copy and partner block. Preserve subject proportions and leave breathing room for alternative crops. Keep the complete car inside the frame. No added captions, watermarks, UI, extra logos or graphic overlays.
